title: Optimizing Agent Reliability and Tool Calling Efficiency for Chip Design Using NVIDIA NeMo Gym | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA and Siemens EDA used the open NeMo Gym evaluation environment to tune the Siemens Fuse EDA AI Agent for standard-cell Liberty file generation, lifting a composite verifier score from about 55% to about 95% while cutting agent turns from 155 to 53 and output tokens from about 81K to 29K. The gains came from refining skills and MCP tool descriptions against a final-artifact verifier, not from changing the model.

insights.claim: In multistage chip design workflows, an undetected early setup error by an AI agent can silently propagate through downstream stages into the final artifact, so reliability is a major barrier to production adoption of agents.
insights.speaker: Joshua Mabry
insights.so_what: Agent adoption in EDA hinges on verification tooling, which favors vendors supplying evaluation infrastructure.
insights.quote: an undetected error early in setup can silently propagate through downstream stages and final artifact generation
insights.locator: AI agents offer remarkable productivity gains

insights.claim: Engineering agents must be evaluated against final artifacts rather than individual tool calls, because end-to-end Liberty verification exposed missing cells and operating conditions, incorrect slew thresholds, and timing or power values outside tolerance that intermediate checks missed.
insights.speaker: Joshua Mabry
insights.so_what: Benchmarks that grade only tool-call success overstate agent reliability; prefer products validated on final outputs.

insights.claim: Errors in the characterization workflow often produce plausible outputs instead of clean failures, leaving incorrect thresholds, missing corners or incomplete cells hidden.
insights.speaker: Joshua Mabry
insights.so_what: Silent failure modes imply human-in-the-loop and verifier cost remain necessary in chip design automation.
insights.locator: Errors often produce plausible outputs instead of clean failures

insights.claim: The Siemens verifier scores Liberty outputs as a product of binary gates for coverage, validity, relative validation and integrity multiplied by the fraction of timing and power values within tolerance, so the reward is zero if any gate fails.
insights.speaker: Joshua Mabry
insights.so_what: Gated multiplicative rewards are a reusable pattern for RL environments in engineering domains.
insights.quote: The reward is zero if any gate fails.

insights.claim: A domain-specific grader should detect missing, truncated, reformatted or reused results to prevent agent cheating, and the same final-artifact evaluation method applies to engineering agents in EDA, CAE and other domains.
insights.speaker: Joshua Mabry
insights.so_what: Signals NVIDIA positioning NeMo Gym as a cross-vertical engineering-agent evaluation layer beyond chip design.
insights.locator: Developing reliable agents in other domains using the same method

insights.claim: After refining skills and MCP tool descriptions, the mean composite verification score for the Solido Characterization Suite agent rose from approximately 55% to approximately 95% on a standard-cell characterization benchmark.
insights.speaker: Joshua Mabry
insights.so_what: Harness and tool-description tuning, with the model held fixed, delivered a large reliability gain.

insights.claim: The same tuning cut agent turns from 155 to 53 (about 66%) and average output tokens from about 81K to 29K (about 64%), improving efficiency per successful result.
insights.speaker: Joshua Mabry
insights.so_what: Lower turns and tokens per task reduce inference cost, strengthening the ROI case for agentic EDA.

insights.claim: The tuning benchmark used the open source GF180MCU PDK (229 standard cells across 36 PVT corners) but each run was restricted to two cells across 36 corners, took about 1.5 to 2 hours, and about 25 rollouts were run with Claude Opus 4.8 in Claude Code as the fixed model and harness.
insights.speaker: Joshua Mabry
insights.so_what: The results are from a small development subset, so generalization to full libraries is unproven.
insights.locator: The team used the open source GF180MCU PDK

themes.theme: Optimization loop for skills and MCP tools

insights.claim: The optimization loop runs versioned baseline rollouts, inspects trajectories and verifier diagnostics, refines skills and MCP tool descriptions, and reruns under identical conditions, driven by a coding agent with a human in the loop.
insights.speaker: Joshua Mabry
insights.so_what: Agent performance is increasingly a function of tool-interface design, creating tooling opportunities around evaluation.
insights.locator: This enabled engineers to run the following optimization loop

insights.claim: To improve tool selection the team simplified overlapping file and shell interfaces and defined tool inputs with explicit JSON schemas, making characterization tools easier for the agent to call.
insights.speaker: Joshua Mabry
insights.so_what: Clear, non-overlapping tool schemas are a cheap lever for agent reliability.

insights.claim: Siemens Fuse EDA AI Agent exposes MCP servers and skills for the Solido Characterization Suite to common coding harnesses including Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, and standard-cell characterization must be redone for every affected cell whenever a foundry updates a PDK.
insights.speaker: Joshua Mabry
insights.so_what: PDK refresh cycles create recurring characterization workload that agentic automation targets.
insights.locator: The Solido Characterization Suite agent automates this process
